query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the spray stand-off distance will increase the coating thickness of an FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock while maintaining coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl bond coat using standard 15–45 μm feedstock deposited via thermal spraying at a baseline stand-off distance (e.g., ~100 mm).
generation.intervention: Reduce the spray stand-off distance to approximately 70 mm.
generation.conditions: Thermal spraying under identical gas composition and substrate preheat settings as the baseline, performed in an inert or controlled atmosphere; service conditions typical for TBC bond coats (high temperature, cyclic thermal loading).
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced particle kinetic energy on impact leading to improved splat flattening and reduced particle scattering.
generation.mechanism: A shorter stand-off distance reduces the time particles spend in the oxidizing environment, minimizing in-flight oxidation and maintaining higher impact velocities that favor thicker, denser coatings.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coating thickness increases by approximately 30–50% relative to the baseline deposit, with oxide content remaining at or below baseline levels and with similar microstructural integrity.
generation.baseline: Deposits made with 15–45 μm feedstock at ~100 mm stand-off distance resulting in insufficient thickness and moderate oxidation.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is expected provided that the reduced distance does not induce splashing or substrate overheating; operational parameters must remain within the thermal spray equipment limits.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal distance may vary with feedstock dispersion and equipment configuration; slight increases in residual stress or micro-cracking could occur if the distance is too short.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of thermal spray depositions on FeCoNiCrAl bond coats at varying stand-off distances (e.g., 70 mm, 85 mm, 100 mm) while keeping all other parameters constant. Measure the final coating thickness, oxide content via XRD/EDS, and assess microstructural integrity using SEM.
measurements: Microstructural analysis via SEM/EDS for defects
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reduction in stand-off distance does not result in a statistically significant increase (≥30%) in coating thickness, or if the oxide content increases relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.2. Oxidation and Phase Transformations in the Powder during HVOF Spraying
cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). It is known [] that when Al concentration in FeCoNiCrAlMo0.5 is lower than 10%, FCC solid solution becomes preferable to BCC. The roughness of the thermal sprayed coatings can be adjusted by optimizing the parameters while spraying that include stand-off distance, power, voltage, and feedstock morphology as reported by Anupam et al. []. Li, Zuhao, et al. reported that the roughness of the alloy improved after the heat treatment []. In the case of plasma-sprayed samples, the roughness values were found to be higher than that of annealed coatings. Different particles experience different heating temperatures during flight and projection towards substrate thus forming splats on the substrate surface upon complete or partial melting. These partially melted particles forming splats upon cooling give rise to higher values of roughness. While in the case of annealing treatment of coatings the roughness values were found to be lowered, this is consistent with the diffusion process as the temperature applied in annealing favored the alloy formation and grain refinement which resulted in a fine microstructure and lower roughness values. papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder.
papers.system: FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy (HEA) powder used in HVOF deposition.
papers.approach: Systematic variation of spraying distance during high-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) deposition to study in‐flight oxidation and phase transformations.
papers.findings: Longer spray distances led to slightly decreased coating thickness, increased porosity, and more extensive oxidation. In-flight oxidation resulted in Al depletion (yielding a phase shift from the BCC solid solution to FCC) due to longer particle residence and exposure to oxygen.
papers.mechanism: Longer flight times reduce particle kinetic energy at impact and increase oxygen exposure, promoting oxidation and altering phase stability via aluminum depletion.

papers.title: Microstructural Evolution of AlCoCrFeNiSi High-Entropy Alloy Powder during Mechanical Alloying and Its Coating Performance.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy processed by mechanical alloying and deposited by atmospheric plasma spraying (APS).
papers.approach: Optimization of feedstock powder properties (including particle size distribution and morphology) to achieve consistent splat formation and coating integrity during APS.
papers.findings: Feedstock milled to an optimum duration (10 h) showed near-equiaxed, well‐flowing powder leading to uniform splat formation and a dense, even coating structure. Particle shape and size distribution were key in ensuring adhesion and consistency of the deposit.
papers.mechanism: Controlled particle melting and rapid solidification during APS are critical; a well‑defined particle size distribution ensures sufficient kinetic energy transfer and minimizes unmelted regions, impacting overall coating thickness and microstructure.

papers.title: Microstructure and Corrosion Behavior of Atmospheric Plasma Sprayed NiCoCrAlFe High Entropy Alloy Coating.
papers.system: NiCoCrAlFe-based high-entropy alloy deposited via atmospheric plasma spraying (APS).
papers.approach: Variation of APS process parameters—including stand‐off distance and feedstock morphology—to tailor phase composition and manage in-flight oxidation, followed by post-deposition annealing for property optimization.
papers.findings: As-sprayed coatings consisted of mixed BCC and FCC phases with variable oxide content. Shorter in-flight times (influenced by spray distance) tended to yield denser coatings with reduced oxidation levels and improved adhesion, while annealing further refined the microstructure and corrosion behavior.
papers.mechanism: Spray parameters determine the kinetic energy of particles and exposure time to the oxidizing environment; shorter distances increase deposition efficiency and reduce oxidation, while the rapid melting–splatting process governs microstructure formation.

established: Longer in-flight times (i.e., larger spray distances) lead to increased oxidation and lower particle kinetic energy upon impact, reducing coating thickness.
In-flight oxidation influences phase composition (e.g., aluminum depletion drives BCC-to-FCC transitions) and can enhance wear resistance if controlled.

Feedstock powder properties (size, shape, and distribution) and spray parameters (stand-off distance, feed rate) are key determinants of coating microstructure, density, and overall deposition efficiency.

approaches_tried.approach: Varying spray distance in HVOF deposition.
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that shorter spray distances can increase particle kinetic energy, reducing in-flight oxidation time and enhancing coating thickness; longer distances conversely lead to thinner, more porous coatings.

approaches_tried.approach: Optimizing feedstock powder characteristics via mechanical alloying.
approaches_tried.outcome: Establishing an optimum particle size and morphology led to improved flowability and uniform splat formation in APS, indirectly benefiting coating integrity and deposition efficiency.

approaches_tried.approach: Tuning APS parameters such as stand-off distance and plasma power.
approaches_tried.outcome: Enables control over in-flight oxidation and densification; demonstrated potential to achieve lower oxidation while maintaining coating adhesion.

mechanisms: Control of particle kinetic energy: Shorter spray distances yield higher impact velocities and reduce flight time, limiting oxidation.
In-flight oxidation dynamics: Longer exposure to oxygen promotes oxide formation which can alter phase composition (e.g., via Al depletion) and affect deposit density.
Splat formation and rapid solidification: The melting state and particle interactions during impact determine coating microstructure and adhesion.
disagreements: Some studies highlight that a controlled amount of in-flight oxidation may be beneficial for enhancing hardness and wear resistance, while others argue that minimal oxidation is essential for maintaining coating integrity—highlighting a trade-off.

There is not complete consensus on the optimal spray distance; although shorter distances can improve thickness, they may also risk issues with excessive particle velocity or splashing in some process setups.
open_questions: What is the optimal single process intervention that can robustly increase coating thickness for FeCoNiCrAl bond coats while preserving coating integrity and minimizing as-sprayed oxidation?
How do subtle changes in spray distance versus feed rate or powder size specifically affect the deposition efficiency for FeCoNiCrAl alloy systems?
Can strategies proven in other HEA systems (e.g., FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 or NiCoCrAlFe) be directly translated to FeCoNiCrAl bond coats in thermal barrier coating applications?
opportunities: Investigate a targeted reduction in spray stand-off distance as a single intervention to increase particle kinetic energy and reduce flight time, thereby promoting thicker deposits with less oxidation.
Experiment with controlled modification of powder feed rate to supplement the increased deposition efficiency obtained by a reduced stand-off distance.
Consider systematic experiments combining a shorter spray distance with well-characterized feedstock powder properties to establish a process window that meets the thickness and oxidation criteria.
Develop a controlled experiment that isolates spray distance as the variable with thickness and oxidation levels as measurable outcomes to verify the efficacy of this intervention.

directions.assessment: Directly increases particle kinetic energy by shortening flight time, thereby reducing in‐flight oxidation and splat scattering. Evidence shows that shorter spray distances yield thicker, denser coatings with lower oxidation [PMC10820071::web::010::3_2_oxidation_and_phase_transformations_]. It respects the requirement of preserving coating integrity, though care must be taken to avoid excessive particle impact that might induce splashing.

directions.direction: Adjust the feedstock particle size distribution toward larger average diameters within the 15–45 μm range
directions.assessment: Increasing the lower bound of particle size should enhance deposition efficiency because larger particles have higher momentum and less relative oxidation. Prior studies optimizing powder morphology [PMC5849017::web::015::3_1_1_surface_morphology_and_particle_si] support that particle size distribution is critical for forming uniform splats. However, the trade-off between melting and oxidation must be balanced to preserve integrity.

directions.direction: Increase the powder feed rate during the spray process
directions.assessment: A higher feed rate delivers more material per unit time to the substrate, potentially increasing the deposit thickness. This intervention targets the thickness shortfall directly, and literature indicates that feed rate influences cladding thickness [PMC11857518::web::013::3_2_dilution_rate_mathematical_model_and]. It must be optimized to avoid destabilizing the melt pool, ensuring minimal oxidation and good bonding.

directions.direction: Incorporate an inert gas shroud at the nozzle exit
directions.assessment: A short burst of inert gas (e.g., argon) surrounding the spray plume minimizes oxygen ingress during particle flight, thus reducing in‐flight oxidation. This technique has been discussed in the context of controlling oxidation during thermal spraying [PMC8875499::web::002::1_introduction]. It is a single intervention that can be combined with current process parameters to ensure thicker deposits with preserved coating integrity.

candidates.hypothesis: Increasing the powder feed rate during thermal spraying will result in a thicker FeCoNiCrAl bond coat while maintaining coating integrity and low as-sprayed oxidation.

candidates.hypothesis: Integrating an inert gas shroud at the nozzle exit will decrease in-flight oxidation and improve the deposition efficiency, resulting in a thicker FeCoNiCrAl bond coat with maintained coating integrity.
candidates.intervention: Introduce a localized inert gas (argon) shroud at the nozzle exit to envelop the spray plume during deposition.
